info.title: The Skills & Practices Framework API
info.summary: An open, machine-readable map of how people work well together.
info.description: A static, read-only API over the Skills & Practices Framework. Every endpoint is a JSON file served by GitHub Pages, so it is free and always available. Field names are the framework's own; see schema/context.jsonld for the schema.org and SKOS mapping. Data is licensed CC BY 4.0 (credit Tech Fleet); the code is Apache-2.0.

example.Data Type Description: A competency in an area of expertise.
example.Relationship to Skills:
Skills and other Skills are related in the following ways:
1. Some skills are prerequisites that people build before they can pick up more advanced skills.
2. Growing one skill often strengthens the related skills a person already has.
example.Relationship to Practices:
Skills and Practices are related in the following ways:
1. People need practices like shared ownership and psychological safety to use their skills well on a team.
2. Practices shape how a person applies a skill with others, so the same skill lands differently depending on the practices behind it.
example.Relationship to Projects:
Skills and Projects are related in the following ways:
1. People use their skills to move a project forward and get the work done.
2. Projects give people a real place to apply and prove their skills.
example.Relationship to Duties:
Skills and Duties are related in the following ways:
1. People need certain skills to take on a duty and handle its responsibilities.
2. A duty defines which skills a person is expected to bring and keep growing.
example.Relationship to Stakeholders:
Skills and Stakeholders are related in the following ways:
1. People use their skills to understand and meet what stakeholders need.
2. Stakeholders drive the demand for specific skills by shaping what the work requires.
example.Relationship to Milestones:
Skills and Milestones are related in the following ways:
1. People must have the right skills to reach a milestone in the work.
2. Each milestone calls for a particular set of skills before a team can complete it.
example.Relationship to Tools:
Skills and Tools are related in the following ways:
1. People rely on their skills to use tools effectively.
2. Tools extend a person's skills and usually take skill to operate well.
example.Relationship to Activities:
Skills and Activities are related in the following ways:
1. People apply their skills to carry out the day-to-day activities of the work.
2. Doing activities over and over is how people build and sharpen their skills.
example.Relationship to Deliverables:
Skills and Deliverables are related in the following ways:
1. People use their skills to create the deliverables a team produces.
2. Each deliverable calls for specific skills to make it well.
example.Relationship to Job Functions:
Skills and Job Functions are related in the following ways:
1. People qualify for a job function by having the skills it calls for.
2. A job function points to the skills a person is expected to have.
example.Relationship to Job Specializations:
Skills and Job Specializations are related in the following ways:
1. A specialization is built on a focused set of skills a person grows deep in.
2. The skills you choose to sharpen point you toward a specialization.
example.Relationship to Company Types:
Skills and Company Types are related in the following ways:
1. The skills a person has help them fit the way different company types work.
2. Different company types lean on different skills, so the setting shapes which skills matter most.
example.Relationship to Methodologies:
Skills and Methodologies are related in the following ways:
1. People apply their skills within a methodology to guide how the work flows.
2. A methodology calls for certain skills, like facilitation or planning, to run it well.
example.Relationship to Workshops:
Skills and Workshops are related in the following ways:
1. People bring and use their skills to take part in workshops.
2. Workshops are a hands-on way for people to build and practice skills together.
example.Tech Job Categories: User Experience, Product Management, Development, Operations, Information Technology
example.Relationship to Job Industries:
Skills and Job Industries are related in the following ways:
1. People carry transferable skills with them from one industry into another.
2. Each industry gives people a starting set of skills shaped by its everyday work.

get.description: Returns the full Skills dataset (115 records) as a JSON array. Each relationship is a {slug, label} reference to another record. The example below shows one representative record.

example.Example of the Skill: Imagine interviewing is like being a detective who asks people about their day to figure out what makes them happy or frustrated, just like Sherlock Holmes asking questions to solve a mystery.
example.How the Skill is Carried Out Daily: In a UX Research job, interviewing is done by talking to real users, either in person or online, and asking them about how they use an app or website. The researcher listens carefully, takes notes, and tries to understand what users like, what confuses them, and what problems they face. This involves making users feel comfortable (psychological safety), making decisions about what to ask (decision-making), taking responsibility for the process (ownership), and working with others to make sure everyone’s ideas are heard (service leadership, self-organization, empowerment).
example.Importance of the Skill: Interviewing is important in UX Research because it helps teams learn what users really need and want. This information is used to make products easier and more enjoyable to use, which means happier customers and better results for the company.
example.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

example.Difference between Practices and Skills:
Practices:
1. A practice requires working with other people
1. A practice never stops being built; you never become an expert in a practice, but the behaviors of a practice become more permanent over time
1. A practice is rooted in beliefs and behaviors
1. A practice can be measured through what other people believe about you
1. A practice cannot be concretely measured through deliverables
1. A practice is an intentional choice someone makes to do
1. You learn how to get good about your practice by reflecting to yourself
1. A practice can be measured through what you believe about yourself
1. You learn how to get good about your practice by reflecting with others
Skills:
1. A skill enables you to make a deliverable
1. A skill is measured through how many times you have applied it
1. A skill is rooted in  knowledge and theory
1. A skill applies to a specific activity
1. A skill is expected to be performed in specific job functions
1. A skill is something someone can become an expert in it with a lot of experience
1. A skill you can perform yourself
1. A skill can be practiced by applying it to work you deliver or duties you perform
1. A skill is required in specific jobs, people may not have a choice to perform the skill if the job requires them
1. A skill gets practiced by doing work and performing duties

What they both have in common: 
1. A practice and a skill can be lost if  not continued to be practiced
1. A practice and a skill require willingness to perform
example.Practice Level 0 Definition:
1. You are not aware of what makes up the practice
1. You are not willing to practice it
1. You tried to practice it, but stopped
example.Practice Level 1 Definition:
1. You believe it's valuable to practice the practice
1. You are willing to practice it
1. You have knowledge about the components of the practice
1. You've started practicing with others and reflecting
example.Practice Level 2 Definition:
1. You've seen growth in your own practice through reflection
1. You are starting to work on changing habits
example.Practice Level 3 Definition:
1. Your habits are starting to become automatic in your practice with others
1. You’re so practiced in it, that you are a role model to others in the practice
1. You can and do advocate for the practice when working with others

example.What Mindset Do You Have When You Practi: At its core, Shared Ownership comes from believing a team is stronger when responsibility is spread around. You trust that other people are capable, even when they are still learning, and you are willing to let go of control so they can lead. You also stay honest with yourself about where you can grow, and you treat every teammate's contribution as genuinely valuable.
example.What Habits Do You Hold When You Practic: In everyday work, this looks like handing off meaningful work instead of hoarding it, and encouraging people who try even when they fall short. You set clear expectations so others can run with the work, admit your own mistakes openly, and make room for teammates to lead on things you could easily have kept for yourself.
example.Practice Description: Shared Ownership is the idea that the work belongs to everyone on the team, not just whoever was handed a task. When a team practices it, people step up for problems even when they are not officially theirs, and they trust each other to carry real responsibility. It is built from smaller habits like humility, delegation, and a growth mindset, and it deepens over time until sharing the load feels natural. On a healthy team, no one says 'that is not my job.'
example.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

example.Assessment Question: I do not judge myself or others, I operate without dominance or arrogance
example.Component Description: Humility means treating yourself and everyone around you as equals, with no need to dominate or prove you are the smartest in the room. On a team it frees you to admit you do not have all the answers and to stay open to being wrong, which is exactly what lets a group share ownership and take turns leading. It is quiet, but it is the ground that Shared Ownership and Shared Leadership grow in.
example.Associated Mindsets of the Component: You believe your way is not the only right way, and that every person, no matter how new, has something to teach you. Being wrong is not a threat; it is a chance to learn.
example.Associated Habits of the Component: You hold back quick judgment, own your mistakes out loud, and give credit to others instead of taking it for yourself.
example.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

example.Activity Description: Wireframing is sketching the bare-bones layout of a screen, showing where things go without color or polish. It is about structure, not looks.
example.Why Is This Activity Important?: Starting rough lets the team test and change ideas cheaply before anyone builds a finished-looking design.
example.How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens during the Implement work and produces wireframes that grow into prototypes. Teams often wireframe together in a workshop so everyone shapes the layout.
example.How To Complete the Activity: Start from the user's task and block out where each piece goes on the screen. Use a tool like Figma or FigJam to lay out simple boxes, then share it for quick feedback.
example.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

example.Duty Description: The UX Design duty is about shaping how a product actually works for the people using it, turning rough ideas into screens and flows that feel simple. Day to day that means sketching wireframes, building clickable prototypes, and pulling patterns together into a design system so the whole product feels like one coherent thing. Designers rarely work in a straight line; they try something, put it in front of people, and refine it as the team learns.
example.What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes a mix of craft and people skills: interaction design, information architecture, and prototyping to build the work, plus the openness to share ownership and take feedback without ego. Comfort in tools like Figma and Figjam helps, but the real skill is staying curious about whether a design truly makes sense for a real person.
example.Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: Design is where a plan becomes something people can see and touch. This duty owns deliverables like wireframes and prototypes that the rest of the team builds on, and it stays active from early discovery through launch, so the product keeps improving instead of freezing at version one.
You might enjoy this duty if you like turning fuzzy problems into clear, usable designs, enjoy sketching and iterating, and get satisfaction from watching a rough idea become something people find easy to use.
example.Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

example.Job Function Description: A UX Designer shapes how a product looks, feels, and works for the people who use it. Most days you take fuzzy ideas and turn them into screens and flows that feel simple and clear. You sketch, try layouts, and put your work in front of others to get feedback, always asking whether it makes sense for a real person. It is a blend of creative and practical work, and you do it shoulder to shoulder with researchers, writers, and engineers.
example.Other Job Titles You May See in the Worl: Product Designer, Interaction Designer, UI/UX Designer, Experience Designer, Digital Product Designer
You may like this job function if you enjoy turning fuzzy ideas into clear, usable screens, like sketching and refining based on feedback, and care about how something works as much as how it looks. It suits people who are part creative and part practical, and who are happy collaborating with researchers, writers, and engineers.

example.Deliverable Description: A vision board is a simple, visual snapshot of where a product is headed and the future it is trying to create. Teams use it to capture the big idea in a form everyone can see and rally around before diving into the details.
example.Why Is This Deliverable Important?: It gives the team a shared thing to aim at, so day-to-day choices line up with the larger goal instead of drifting apart.
example.How Does This Deliverable Relate to Othe: It takes shape during the Vision milestone and sets the direction that later work like the roadmap, epics, and scope grows out of. Teams often revisit it as they learn more.

example.Milestone Description: Continuous Discovery is the practice of staying connected to the people a team is building for, instead of guessing what they need. Throughout a project the team keeps interviewing users, digging into problems, and testing its assumptions, and it turns what it hears into clear problem statements and a read on the competition. The name says it plainly: this is continuous. You learn a little at a time, all the way through, so the team is never designing in the dark.
example.Why Is This Milestone Important?: When teams stop listening, they start guessing, and guesses are expensive to build. Ongoing discovery helps the team rule out weak ideas early and lean into the strong ones, so the work stays pointed at problems that genuinely matter to the people using the product.
example.When Should You Do This Milestone In Pro: Discovery does not wait its turn and it never really ends. Teams run it while they are building and even after a launch, and they lean on it hardest whenever they hit a question only a user can answer. Like every milestone here, it is not a step in a line. It runs alongside the others and comes back around many times.
example.Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

example.What Makes This Specialization Unique?: What makes this specialization unique is its focus on understanding people's emotions and experiences, rather than just numbers and data. Unlike other research roles that might focus on statistics, Qualitative UX Research is all about the stories and feelings behind user interactions. It's like being a storyteller who helps design better products by understanding what users truly need and want.

example.When Is This Method Used?: Reach for a Design Sprint when you have one big, risky question and need a real answer fast, before pouring months into building. It shines when a team is unsure which direction to take and wants to test an idea with actual users in days rather than quarters. It is also a quick way to get a group aligned, since everyone works through the problem together in the same room.
example.Who Created This Method?: The Design Sprint was created by Jake Knapp at Google in 2010, then refined with John Zeratsky and Braden Kowitz at Google Ventures (GV). The three shared the full process in their 2016 book, Sprint. Official source: gv.com/sprint.
example.How Does This Method Compare to to Other: Unlike Scrum and Kanban, which run continuously, a Design Sprint is a short, one-week burst aimed at answering a single question. It shares the fast, test-driven spirit of Lean UX and Continuous Discovery but packs it into a fixed five-day structure. Teams often use a sprint to kick off an idea, then hand it to a Scrum or Kanban team for ongoing delivery.
example.During While Kinds of Work Environments: A Design Sprint works best when a team faces one big question or opportunity and needs a tested answer fast, before committing months of work. It fits small, cross-functional teams that can clear a full week and get access to real users. It is a strong fit for startups and new product bets.
example.Steps to Perform the Method:
The Design Sprint runs over five days:
1. Monday: map the problem and choose one target to focus on.
2. Tuesday: sketch competing solutions on your own.
3. Wednesday: decide on the strongest ideas and turn them into a storyboard.
4. Thursday: build a realistic prototype.
5. Friday: test the prototype with about five real users and learn what works.

example.Workshop Summary: The team gets together at the start of a project to get to know each other as people, not just coworkers. Everyone shares things like their interests, how they like to work, what they are excited about, and what worries them. This helps the team feel safe with each other before the real work starts.
example.Workshop Goals:
Help teammates get to know each other as people
Start building trust and psychological safety
Learn how each person likes to work
example.Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Complete four activities with your team.
2. Follow the instructions in each activity section.
3. Run the intro activity: give time to fill out the template, then go around and share out loud.
4. Do the working style activity: place your name where you align on each scale.
5. Add hopes and fears to sticky notes, discuss briefly or invite people to review other’s sticky notes.
6. Run Crazy 6: draw six things about yourself. Invite people to explain their drawings and share anything they want to share.
7. Time-box each activity but leave space for natural banter and questions.
8. Have fun! It's okay if not everything gets done. The goal is team connection.
example.Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: People do better work when they feel comfortable with the people around them. Starting with a human connection makes it easier to speak up, ask for help, and share ideas later in the project.
example.How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Run this once at the start of a new team or project phase. You can also do a short version any time new people join the team.
example.Who Owns the Workshop?: The Agile Coaching function owns this workshop and is responsible for running it with the team.
example.Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have a shared understanding of each other teammate, their background, their interest, and their working styles.
example.Additional Details: When to use: at kickoff, in the first week, before the team digs into project work.
example.Workshop Pitch Statement: A casual first-day kickoff party where a new team gets to know each other as humans, laying the psychological safety and trust the next several weeks of work depend on.
example.What You Need Before You Start: This is the team's very first workshop, so no project prep is needed, just everyone present and willing to be a little playful. Set up the FigJam board with the four activity sections ready to copy, and bring a timer. An Agile Coach should be ready to facilitate and go first to set the tone.
example.The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. Who are my teammates as people?
2. How does each of us like to work, learn, decide, and get feedback?
3. What are our hopes and fears for this project?
4. What do we want to learn, and how can Tech Fleet support us?
example.What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave knowing each other as people, with a first layer of trust and openness in place. Done well, people laughed, shared a little of themselves, and feel safer speaking up. It is fine if not every activity finishes; connection is the goal.
example.Time Needed: About 45 to 60 minutes across the four activities
example.Common Pitfalls & Tips: Do not over-formalize it; the point is fun and connection, not productivity. Time-box each activity but leave room for natural banter. Facilitators should go first and share openly to make it safe for everyone else.
example.Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; it becomes a living memento of the team's start.

# PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT MILESTONES FOR DIFFERENT TYPES OF PROJECTS
  TEAM ICE BREAKER KICKOFF PARTY INSTRUCTIONS
  WHAT IS THIS?
  STEPS TO RUN THE WORKSHOP
  Complete four activities with your team.

Do the working style activity: place your name where you align on each scale.

  This is the first workshop your team will do together. It’s a casual kickoff designed to help everyone connect as humans before diving into project work. At TechFleet, we believe psychological safety is the foundation of great teams and this workshop creates the space to begin building that. By getting to know each other, we also begin cultivating a culture of servant leadership that will carry us through the rest of the project.
  GOALS OF THE WORKSHOP
  Get to know your teammates and build a foundation of psychological safety for the next 11 weeks.
Foster a sense of trust and openness within the team.
Encourage informal communication and camaraderie to enhance collaboration and productivity.
  WHY IS IT VALUABLE?
  Psychological safety is the foundation of a strong Agile team. It enables team members to feel safe, have fun, and be more productive, ultimately fostering better cross-functional collaboration.
  WHO OWNS THIS WORK?
  Agile Coaches own this workshop. They facilitate the team’s initial bonding, foster psychological safety, and ensure everyone feels comfortable and included. By doing so, they lay the groundwork for effective collaboration and communication throughout the project.

example.Summary of the Gaps: Academia trained you in the exact heart of this path: designing studies, running them, and making sense of what you find. Research Facilitation, Experiment Design, and Research Analysis carry over almost whole, so your gap is smaller than most. What changes is the pace and the purpose. Instead of research that stands on its own over months, you run lean studies that feed a product decision this week, and you share rough findings early rather than polishing a paper. The tools are new, mostly Figma, Dovetail, and FigJam, and usability testing will be a fresh method on top of the ones you know.
example.Training Recommendations: You already research well, so aim your energy at speed and application. Learn usability testing and how to choose a method quickly for the question at hand. Pick up Dovetail and Maze to run and analyze studies the way product teams do. Practice turning a study into a short, decision-ready summary instead of a full report. Learn an agile method like Lean UX to feel the faster rhythm. Lean on the rigor you already have while you adjust to working in days, not semesters.
example.A Day in the Life: On a cross-functional team, your day revolves around understanding users. You carry out and see through the research itself: planning studies, recruiting and interviewing people, running usability tests and surveys, and making sense of it all through analysis and heuristics. You turn that into research reports, affinity maps, journey maps, and clear findings the team can act on. Beyond the work you own, you are consulted across almost everything the team builds, weighing in on wireframes, prototypes, content, product strategy, and go-to-market thinking, since your read on real user needs sharpens other people's decisions. A typical day mixes focused sessions, a couple of interviews or a usability test, with synthesis in Dovetail and collaboration: a standup, a design critique where you carry the user's voice, and a working session to plan the next study. You share findings early and often, and you let evidence guide the team rather than opinion.

example.Summary of the Gaps: Academia gave you deep research and writing habits, and the discipline to structure a complex argument, which helps when you organize a product's information. Research Analysis and Written Communication transfer. The bigger change here is the visual, hands-on craft: wireframing, prototyping, and shaping screens and flows, built on Interaction Design and Information Architecture. Your daily surface becomes Figma and FigJam rather than documents. The shift is from explaining ideas in words to showing them as things people can click, and from long solo work to fast, shared drafts.
example.Training Recommendations: Point your structured thinking at the making side. Start with Information Architecture, which rewards organizing complex material, then Interaction Design. Learn wireframing and prototyping in Figma on a real screen. Study a few strong design systems to see how the pieces fit. Learn Lean UX for the team rhythm. Lean on your writing to keep interfaces clear while the visual craft grows.
example.A Day in the Life: On a cross-functional team, your day is spent designing the screens and flows people use. You carry out and see through the making: wireframing layouts, building UI components and kits, developing information architecture, and turning ideas into clickable prototypes, with annotations that tell developers how it should behave. Beyond the screens you own, you are consulted across the team's work, weighing in on research, requirements, content, and product strategy, since design choices touch all of it. A typical day mixes focused design time in Figma and FigJam, sketching, wireframing, and refining a prototype, with collaboration: a standup, a critique where you show rough work for feedback, and a working session with researchers or engineers to keep the design grounded in real needs and buildable. You share drafts early and rough, and you refine in short loops rather than perfecting alone.

example.Summary of the Gaps: In business analysis you are responsible for gathering and writing requirements, running intake with stakeholders, and drafting user stories and acceptance criteria, and you are accountable for those flowing cleanly into wireframes, prototypes, and the experience itself. Academia set you up for the thinking part: Research Analysis, Written Communication, and Problem-Solving all transfer, and structuring a dense argument is close to structuring requirements. What is new is the agile machinery, user stories, acceptance criteria, and BDD scenarios, plus working live with a team in Notion, FigJam, and Trello at a faster pace than a paper allows.
example.Training Recommendations: Start with Requirements Management, the first step and the spine of the role. Learn to write user stories and acceptance criteria in a clear, testable way, since those are your core outputs. Practice an intake conversation that turns a vague request into a scoped problem. Because you are accountable for what comes after, learn enough wireframing and customer experience mapping to guide the design even when others draw it. Pick up Notion and Trello, and learn Scrum for the rhythm. Lean on your research and writing while the agile artifacts become familiar.
example.A Day in the Life: On a cross-functional team, your day is spent turning fuzzy needs into a clear, agreed picture of what to build. You carry out the core requirements work: running intake and kickoff conversations, gathering and refining requirements, writing user stories and acceptance criteria, and framing the problems worth solving. You are also accountable for what those requirements become, making sure they flow cleanly into wireframes, prototypes, customer experience maps, and SEO, so what gets built matches what was agreed. Beyond that, you are consulted across nearly the whole team, from research and design to development and go-to-market, since almost every decision touches what to build and why. A typical day mixes focused writing, drafting stories and acceptance criteria in Notion and Trello, with a lot of conversation: a standup, a refinement session, and working time with designers, engineers, and stakeholders to keep everyone aligned. You work in short loops, share drafts early, and adjust as the team learns.

example.Summary of the Gaps: As a product owner you are responsible for defining feature vision and scope, planning sprints, setting priorities, and maintaining the backlog, and you are accountable for the work shipping as agreed, from problem statements through acceptance testing. Academia gave you the ability to frame big questions and analyze deeply, which helps you shape vision and judge what matters. Research Analysis and Problem-Solving transfer. What is new is the agile ownership craft, backlog management, sprint planning, and epics, plus the business sense to prioritize by value, worked in Notion and Trello.
example.Training Recommendations: Start with Vision Formation and Backlog Management, the first steps and the core of the role. Learn to write and order a backlog, and to run sprint planning. Practice turning a big goal into scoped features and priorities. Since you are accountable for delivery, learn enough about acceptance criteria and QA to know when work is truly done. Pick up Notion and Trello, and learn Scrum. Lean on your analytical framing while the agile craft becomes familiar.
example.A Day in the Life: On a cross-functional team, your day is about deciding what the team builds next and in what order. You carry out the ownership work: defining feature vision and scope, planning sprints, setting priorities, maintaining the product backlog and roadmap, and keeping an eye on competitors. You are accountable for a wide slice of delivery, from problem definition and user stories through QA, acceptance testing, and the sprint demo, making sure what ships is what the team agreed to and what users need. You are consulted across research, design, and engineering, since your priorities shape everyone's work. A typical day mixes backlog and planning work in Notion, Trello, and FigJam with constant conversation: a standup, backlog refinement, a sprint planning or demo session, and quick calls to unblock the team. You steer in short loops, reorder the backlog as you learn, and keep the team pointed at the highest-value work.

example.Summary of the Gaps: As a product manager you are responsible for product vision, strategy, priorities, and the roadmap, and you are accountable across the whole delivery, from requirements and design through QA and launch. Academia gave you deep analysis, the ability to frame big questions, and strong writing, which help you shape vision and reason about a market. Research Analysis and Problem-Solving transfer. What is new is the business and go-to-market side, product-market fit, positioning, and pricing, plus the agile machinery for steering delivery, worked in Notion, Trello, and FigJam.
example.Training Recommendations: Start with Vision Formation and Backlog Management, then add Go-to-Market Strategy and Product-Market Fit, the business muscles academia does not build. Practice turning a big idea into a vision, a roadmap, and prioritized work. Because you are accountable across delivery, learn enough of requirements, design, and QA to steer the whole. Pick up Notion and Trello, and learn Scrum. Lean on your analysis while the market and agile sense grow.
example.A Day in the Life: On a cross-functional team, your day is about steering a product: what to build, why, and how it wins. You carry out the strategic and planning work: shaping product vision and go-to-market strategy, defining feature vision and scope, framing problems, setting priorities and the roadmap, running kickoff and sprint planning, researching the market, and positioning the product. Because product management wears many hats, you are accountable for a very wide span of delivery, from requirements, design, and QA through architecture and launch, making sure the whole thing adds up to something users want and the business can sustain. You are consulted across nearly every part of the team. A typical day mixes strategy and planning in Notion, Trello, and FigJam with heavy collaboration: standups, stakeholder alignment, backlog refinement, and working sessions with design, research, and engineering. You steer in short loops, adjust as the market and users teach you, and keep everyone pointed at the highest-value work.

example.Summary of the Gaps: In this role your daily work is shaping brand identity, taking stock of content, and writing copy, and you both carry that work out and see it through to a finished, usable result. It rests on craft like Interaction Design and Information Architecture, and produces pieces like an Editorial Style Guide, Microcopy, and a Content Inventory. Academia set you up for the thinking behind it: Research Facilitation, Research Analysis, and Written Communication all transfer, and turning dense ideas into clear prose is close to good copywriting. What is new is the visual and structural craft, and the tools shift from papers to Figma, Notion, and FigJam. The real adjustment is rhythm, from long solitary study to short loops and shared rough drafts.
example.Training Recommendations: Your research and writing are strong, so aim early energy at the craft you will own. Start with Interaction Design and Information Architecture, the least familiar skills. Practice on the real work, drafting a small brand identity or content inventory rather than reading about it. Since you see this work through to done, learn to shape a full Editorial Style Guide, beyond a single paragraph. Pick up Figma and FigJam on a real task, and learn Lean UX for the team pace. Lean on your writing while the visual craft catches up.
example.A Day in the Life: On a cross-functional team, your day centers on the words and brand of the product. You carry out and see through the core content work: shaping brand identity, taking stock of the product's content in a content inventory, and writing the copy that guides people, from headlines down to the small microcopy on a button. Around that, you are pulled into a wide slice of the team's work as an advisor. You sit in on research sessions and design reviews, weigh in on wireframes, information architecture, and prototypes, and help shape strategy, positioning, and go-to-market thinking so the voice stays consistent everywhere. A typical day mixes focused making, drafting and refining content in Figma and FigJam, with collaboration: a standup, a working session with designers or researchers, and quick reviews where your read on clarity and tone helps other people's work land. example.Summary of the Gaps: As an agile coach you are responsible for facilitating the team's ceremonies, shaping working agreements and roles, and coaching people, and you are accountable for the team steadily getting better at how it works. Academia gave you facilitation, presentation, and a habit of guiding people through ideas, which transfer into running workshops and coaching. Written Communication and Problem-Solving transfer. What is new is the agile craft itself, sprint planning, retros, and method selection, plus the service-leadership stance of guiding rather than instructing, worked in Notion, FigJam, and Trello.
example.Training Recommendations: Start with Agile Method Selection and Kanban Board Management, then learn to run the core ceremonies: planning, retro, and demo. Practice facilitating a real session and coaching one teammate. Since you are accountable for the team improving, learn to read agile maturity and shape working agreements. Pick up FigJam and Trello, and learn Scrum deeply. Lean on your facilitation while you trade lecturing for serving the team.
example.A Day in the Life: On a cross-functional team, your day is about how the team works together, more than what it builds. You carry out and see through the facilitation: running sprint planning, retrospectives, and demos, helping the team set working agreements and clear roles, tracking sprint progress, and coaching people one on one. You produce things like working agreements, a team process map, a psychological safety plan, and agile maturity measurements. You are consulted across the whole team, since improving how people collaborate touches every function. A typical day mixes facilitation, a standup you keep crisp and a planning or retro session you guide, with one-on-one coaching conversations and light tracking in Notion, FigJam, and Trello. You lead by serving the team rather than directing it, help people work through friction, and nudge the group toward better habits in short, steady loops.

example.Summary of the Gaps: As a software engineer you carry out and own the building: writing code, designing databases and APIs, shaping architecture, and handling security and testing. This is a real climb from academia, but your foundation helps more than you might expect. Research Analysis, Logical Thinking, and Problem-Solving are exactly the muscles good programming uses, and the discipline of designing an experiment is close to designing a system. What is new is the whole technical craft, an object-oriented language, databases, APIs, and architecture, plus working in short iterations and committing code in GitHub rather than writing alone.
example.Training Recommendations: Expect this to take real time, and lean on your logical mind. Start by learning one object-oriented language well and the fundamentals of programming. Add databases and REST APIs next, then technical architecture. Layer in security basics and QA testing as you go. Learn Git and GitHub early, since all your work lives there. Learn Scrum for the team rhythm. Your research rigor is a genuine asset; programming rewards careful, logical thinkers.
example.A Day in the Life: On a cross-functional team, your day is spent building and maintaining the software itself. You carry out and own the engineering: writing server-side and front-end code, creating databases and REST APIs, shaping technical architecture, and handling security work like threat modeling and audits, then testing your work and deploying it. You produce code, architecture diagrams, an API library, and QA test plans, all versioned in GitHub. You are consulted across the team, since what is feasible shapes what gets designed and planned, so you weigh in on requirements, design, and estimates. A typical day mixes deep focused coding with collaboration: a standup, a technical design discussion, code review, and working sessions with product and design to keep what is built aligned with what is needed. You work in short iterations, commit often, and improve the system steadily rather than building it all at once.
